summary: The note describes literary and media production workshops spreading through local schools since the 2023 academic year. Teachers, students, a psychologist and a professor explain how making films, podcasts and screenplays builds storytelling, critical thinking, cultural exchange, audio-visual literacy and career skills. It argues the workshops are a lasting shift in learning rather than a passing trend.
one_line: Literary and media production workshops in local schools use film, podcasts and screenplays to build creativity, literacy and collaboration, with educators and students describing the benefits.
key_facts: Maplewood High School launched its first "Digital Storytellers" workshop on September 15, 2023.
Jonathan Edwards, an English teacher and media enthusiast, leads the Maplewood High School "Digital Storytellers" workshop.
Sophia Lorenz, a drama instructor at Riverfall Academy, recently incorporated media production into her curriculum so students can turn narratives into films or podcasts.
Emily Nguyen, a junior at Forest Glen High School, says she was never big on Shakespeare or essays but now uses a camera and editing software to tell stories her way.
Ryan Patel, a senior, says creating media taught him the power of perspective and the importance of representation.
Educational psychologist Dr. Thomas Hartley says storytelling through various media activates multiple cognitive processes, including critical thinking, problem-solving and creative expression.
Maria Gonzalez of Sunset Valley School says the workshops act as a melting pot where kids from different backgrounds share stories and understand each other's narratives.
Gonzalez calls screenplay writing "a gateway": adapting literature into a script teaches character development and dialogue practically.
Edwards believes audio-visual literacy is as fundamental as traditional literacy in a media-saturated world.
Media studies professor Sarah Johnson has seen former workshop students thrive in broadcast and film industries, citing technical skills and team collaboration.
Lorenz and her peers aim to make students informed creators, not just consumers of content.
Hartley suggests that integrating classic literature into media production lets students join a cultural dialogue spanning centuries.
